## 8. Models

### Gold Foil (`lumenary:gold-foil`, models this process)

_From: Bookbinding and fine stationery; when: Gold leaf is ancient, hot stamping from the 19th century; works best on: High contrast pictures and logos._

Foil stamping lays a thin metal film on card wherever a heated die touches it. Here your picture is the die: foil goes where the picture is bright. Crumpled foil is a field of tiny creases, each facing a different way, and so each catches a different part of the room, which is why foil sparkles.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Decide where foil goes with a smoothstep around a threshold, given a slightly ragged edge by a little noise.
2. Show the card’s own colour and a fine grain everywhere else.
3. Build a crumpled height map from ridged noise at three scales, with a slow warp so the creases wander.
4. Read the up and down tilt of each facet to choose a colour from a strip that stands for what a metal sheet reflects.
5. Add a thin brighter rim along the edge of the stamped area.

**The maths:**

$$c=\operatorname{smoothstep}\big(t-0.05,\ t+0.05,\ L_b+\rho\big),\qquad t=1-\tfrac{\text{cover}}{100}$$

_Foil coverage c; ρ is a small noise that roughens the edge._ (primitives: soft-threshold, smooth-noise)

$$h_c=0.6\,R(f_0)+0.3\,R(2.3f_0)+0.1\,R(5.1f_0),\qquad R(f)=1-\lvert 2\,n(f\mathbf x)-1\rvert$$

_Crumple height from ridged noise R; f₀ = 1.5 × the facet slider ÷ the picture width._ (primitives: smooth-noise)

$$t_{\text{env}}=0.5+1.25\,n_y+0.55\,n_x+0.28\,(L-0.5)$$

_Position on the foil’s colour strip from the tilt (n_x, n_y) of the normal and the picture brightness._ (written for this model: specific)

**Dials:** `foil` (Foil) = "gold" (gold, silver, rose); `base` (Card) = "wine" (wine, ink, cream); `cover` (Foil coverage) = 55 [10 to 90]; `crumple` (Crumple) = 65 [0 to 100]; `facet` (Facet size) = 8 [3 to 20]; `invert` (Foil on the dark parts) = false; `seed` (Re-crumple) = 1.

**History:** Gold leaf has decorated manuscripts, icons and temples for thousands of years. Hot foil stamping, pressing metallic film onto a surface with a heated die, developed with industrial printing and now decorates book covers, wedding invitations and packaging. The ridged noise behind the crumple was popularised by the graphics researcher Ken Musgrave.
